Unfortunate. I've been following the work on it occasionally.

On one hand, it seemed like JIT work was really progressing in high gear until SC requested a new PEP. Also unfortunate, as it seemed like part of the hope for the JIT was that it'd counter the performance penalty from free threading.

On the other, it did feel (to me) like with all the fancy (and definitely cool) optimizations it got (automatic refcount operation removal, new type-based specializations, inplace math operations), the macrobenchmark benefits weren't _that_ exciting for a JIT. It definitely has potential for more, maybe with even fancier optimizations like unboxing ints, but the complexity just keeps going up.

> It said that the PEP was "overly optimistic" about user-visible differences with the JIT enabled.

The JIT is technically generated from the same source as the interpreter loop itself, so originally the differences were extremely unlikely, but I imagine the risk just kept going up as new JIT-only paths and optimizations were introduced.

And politically, I feel like SC’s reasoning was just “this side project has landed in main branch almost by accident and has been stewing without oversight ever since, with no stabilization in sight”; and the latest PEP was probably still too vague, with a lot of “here’s more things we can add to the stew” - so I can understand if SC wasn’t satisfied.

I think this is a major issue with requiring a PEP for what's a performance optimization.

JITs are big nasty things that by their nature have to do a lot of things. You are basically saying "Give us a PEP for a new python interpreter and compiler".

What they do is fuzzy by their nature because optimizations are very rarely universally beneficial. It's a game of measuring, looking for regressions, and tackling the biggest problem next for whatever sample applications you have available. You always run into the risk of overfitting on top of all that (You may have made django faster, but you've made flask slower).

This is the sort of thing that, IMO, should not go through the PEP process. It's an implementation detail for the runtime.

Imagine, for example, if the JVM needed a bunch of JEPs for JIT improvements. They'd never get done. Or if any javascript engine needed ECMA acceptance before they could do a new JIT optimization.

> Imagine, for example, if the JVM needed a bunch of JEPs for JIT improvements.

They do:

https://openjdk.org/jeps/197

https://openjdk.org/jeps/515

Not every optimization requires a JEP, but certainly something as big as "add or remove a JIT" would 100% require a JEP.

> Imagine, for example, if the JVM needed a bunch of JEPs for JIT improvements.

FWIW, I definitely can find a bunch of both PEPs and JEPs for internal optimizations, random examples:

https://peps.python.org/pep-0509/

https://openjdk.org/jeps/147

You can find those JEPs, but frankly they are there for 1 of 2 reasons.

1. An outsider to the regular OpenJDK dev team proposing an optimization.

2. Advertising for a cool new performance tweak with potentially large impact.

You'll also notice that the JEP descriptions are very different from PEP descriptions.

Probably the largest JEP for the JVM, Valhalla

https://openjdk.org/jeps/401

Does not have the same level of requirements being asked of the Python JIT. Further, it's well understood that this JEP will "live on main" for quite some time in preview before it's accepted and merged.

What the JEP does, instead, is simply describe the feature and potential risks.

The vast majority of JVM optimizations do not get a JEP.

Fair, I don’t argue with that, I’m not knowledgeable about Java’s processes. Just one thing:

> The vast majority of JVM optimizations do not get a JEP.

In Python too. Still, the JIT really is just a really big thing. I don’t know if there could be a better way to do it, as either 1. You develop it off-branch and… make an enormous PR when you’re done, with risks of getting rejected anyway? Or 2, you allow more experiments on main like Rust, but then you end up with hundreds of minor half-maintained nightly-only features, possibly conflicting with each other, and eventually go through bureaucracy to remove them anyway.

So, I'd grant that it'd probably be a JEP for java (the initial JIT) but not that every change to the JIT would result in a new JEP. Java's JIT, hotspot, was integrated right before they started the JEP process. The JEP for the JIT would likely be pretty boring like "It's a JIT, it does this, in some applications we see this sort of speed up". Much like the AOT JEP https://openjdk.org/jeps/514

The Java governance allows for a lot more open ended projects with follow ups. Not that it's reckless, Valhalla is proof of that, but rather that once something is good enough they are pretty open to just shipping it as a preview feature and refining until it is worthy of being stable.

That's why, for example, we saw ZGC get merged, and then JDK after JDK seeing continuing development and improvement on ZGC (Or G1 for that matter). These GCs were fairly rough on their first release and now they are pretty much best in class.

I see a Python JIT as the same thing. Delivering the infrastructure for a JIT would need a PIP, but I wouldn't put in things like "acceptance criteria" beyond "doesn't break older code". I would expect such a project to get continual updates without PEPs.

> I would expect such a project to get continual updates without PEPs.

Just for completeness: the original JIT PR was merged quite enthusiastically and only after the fact it was pointed out that it should have went through a PEP process [1]. The following PEP 744 was of the “informational” type, and the just-withdrawn PEP 836 was the first “standards track” PEP, which means that (in my understanding) it’s technically the first actual PEP that the SC would formally comment on. So in a way it’s not “can we update the JIT” PEP, but the first real “does SC want this JIT as proposed” PEP.

That said, I do agree with most of what you said, especially the acceptance criteria part.

The issue I have and find it hard to resolve is that since the code was already on main, the feature was already in “sunk cost” mode. It’s hard when the code is already on main and another 3 optimization PRs are always there behind the corner, but it needs to be possible for SC to say “we decided it’s not actually worth all this complexity for % speed improvement” (I’m not commenting whether in this particular case it’d have been a right call), and the PEP (if not withdrawn) was the way to exercise that control.

[1] https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/113465#issuecomment-1...

The original JIT certainly did not get a JEP, because JEPs replaced the previous JSR process.

And even then, Hotspot did not got a JSR, because all that work was done before Sun started collaborating with industry partners for Java evolution.

They "simply" ported the JIT compiler from the Strongtalk acquisition into Java.

Oh, it's not just a performance optimization. But you've said it yourself: "a new python interpreter and compiler". A lot of Python code out there lives with assumptions of CPython interpreter built into it. Pretty sure pytest would've been affected, should JIT replace the existing interpreter, for example.

Anyways. I don't believe that Python needs a JIT compiler. I don't believe that CPython can realistically replace its interpreter with JIT compiler without causing major problems with the community packages.

The way I see it: Python users today desperately want Java. They want it called Python because there's some vague memory still around of Python being cool and Java not being cool.

In Russian there's a children tale about a hungry soldier returning from a war and a greedy old woman who offered him a bed for the night. The old woman then pretends to have no food for dinner, and a soldier promises her a magic trick of making a porridge out of a hatchet. And so he tells the woman to put a pot on a stove with a hatchet in it, and step by step he makes her add all the ingredients necessary to make a porridge to the pot. The story gave birth to the idiom "hatchet porridge", which is used to describe anything that was created in a similar way: by deception, when another goal was allegedly being pursued.

So, to me, the current state of Python is this "hatchet porridge". None of its users want the actual Python (the hatchet is still sticking out of the pot), and they keep adding Java ingredients to the pot in hopes to cook up Java. And so was JIT. It just turned out to be too difficult to throw away the hatchet. An the porridge still has some chipped wood in it as well as a metallic taste.

Just FYI, basically the same story is common in European folklore, and there's a somewhat idiomatic "stone soup" concept in English

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_Soup

Aren’t you confusing internals and API? I don’t think nobody cares about HOW the optimisation is done, but SC wanted API with the rest of the interpreter be defined and stable. Two different things. I think.

I am confused. Why can't they have an experimental, optionally-enabled feature for a few years while they iron out all the issues ? What is wrong with that ? The JDK keeps doing this all the while. They write a new JEP if there are changes across previews.

That works well for greenfield code, but if working on compiler optimisations has taught me anything, it's that there is a lot of legacy code out there in the world that would benefit from re-compilation with optimisations - but would be very difficult to re-write for speed (regardless of whether the work is done by a human, AI, or other machine tool). JIT compilation fits very nicely in this niche, as it means that existing Python projects can get (theoretically) better performance without re-writing.
I've had good success with just using mypyc (https://mypyc.readthedocs.io/en/latest/introduction.html) on typed python code.

> on typed python code.

A fairly massive undertaking for existing code, which jit was supposed to be useful for.

You can use static type analysers and runtime type profilers to add type annotations to a legacy codebase, but the interesting bit would be if you're built on top of a large untyped codebase you don't control like, say, Django, how far it can go.
I would imagine that the LLM has a much easier time adding correct type annotations to old Python code than it does translating it to C.

In my experiments with this, maybe, sorta, it'll do some AST stuff then it'll go "dang this shit is dynamic AF" then suggest a static type inference tool, then a runtime type profiler.

Which honestly, is the right approach.

People have been calling Python a "prototyping" language for decades. I'd be interested to see how many Python projects ever actually get rewritten in a more performant language. My guess is, up until the last five years that was almost never done. Even with LLMs to help, is that the best use of your tokens and humans' time? It doesn't add a feature. It could conceivably cut costs after enough time, but only if done correctly.

> My guess is, up until the last five years that was almost never done.

Because having just the hot loop in the performant language is often deemed good enough. And there's tons of Python code out there where the "hot loop" is already automatically in C (the various operations implemented in C by the runtime) or where you can get close enough e.g. with Numpy. Consider that things like Pygame can exist; for a lot of the games people want to make, the only thing that really needs to happen anywhere near "bare-metal" speed is blitting.

Doing it currently, Python to Go. Early indications are a 50-98% increase in speed (e.g. one testcase went from 26hrs to 30mins) for network/CPU heavy workload. Conversion via Qwem, lots of testing needed but compute savings will be worth it.

It was done plenty. Just with extensions to python like numpy and opencv. There is no reason to translate everything versus just the critical pieces.

This is what happens what the defacto implementation, CPython and its external API, is effectively the specification. That includes all the incidental side effects that were not explicitly designed, but inherited as a quirk of historical implementation. It's next to impossible to retrofit a JIT given these constraints. ECMAScript has a proper specification and several implementations.

Here’s an idea instead (maybe it already exists). Allow a decorator for writing inline Cython. It solves, I think, 90% of the problem. On first run, or eagerly, compile the decorated functions. Basically, Cython is the JIT, and user enables it explicitly.

This way I can easily write inlined functions with proper C speed, in a Python esque language.

Reasons why I rarely use Cython without this:

- unmodified Python code running in Cython is often faster, but not that much. 50% or so is my rule of thumb.

- but the development style is very different for Cython and Python, adding a lot of impedance. Eg reloading doesn’t quite work, profiling is different, you need a build directory and a build step at deployment etc.

- Cython proper is different enough and I’d argue unintuitive enough that if I have to have all these things in place, I might as well wrap my function in Rust.

Such a decorator would give you a low friction way to make things faster when you need it, with scope for making it much faster via all the funny Cython, while keeping Python-esque semantics, in particular "development semantics".

I think it would require some language modification since Cython was definitely a superset of Python; I think some of that syntax has been streamlined, but maybe still a strict superset.

I like Julia approach, compile everything on first launch, then reuse without speed penality, if you change a function, recompile that.

On another note, I'm working on a (big) PEP for python, and looking for maintainers and sponsors (as per python's rules). Do someone know where I could find such amazing persons? (I already have the code, works in cython,graalVM and pypy, and it's kind of a big change but I believe it will help a lot the language)

However because of this, Julia has has persistent problems with "time to first plot", which has gotten better, but they cannot fully ameliorate due to the way it fundamentally works. So there are tradeoffs -- the performance gets better, but the interpreted REPL experience is markedly worse.

By the way, the current nightly (especially if considering the optimized build) has a very substantial TTFX drop compared to the current release [1]

[1] https://perf.julialang.org/?tab=overview

It's not unavoidable, it just hasn't yet been avoided. It could be avoided the same way as other JITs: by interpreting until a compiled version of the code is available. That's actually being worked on, but it adds considerable complexity. Among other things, it requires being able to jump out of an executing interpreter loop into an optimized, compiled version of the same function. Doable, but annoying to implement and requires compiling two versions of the function instead of one. It can also cause performance instability — see https://tratt.net/laurie/blog/2022/more_evidence_for_problem... and the older paper referenced there.

It is overly exaggerated, especially when taken into account how long it takes to compile native libraries that people keep calling "Python" libraries, if there isn't a suitable wheel for the current environment.
I think it's true that it's exaggerated, but that doesn't mean the tradeoff doesn't exist.

A tradeoff that doesn't make sense to complain about, when the alternative is waiting for native libraries being compiled, in a mix of C, C++, Fortran and more recently Rust.

A pain point that is big enough that at least two programming languages, Julia and Mojo, were created to move beyond it.

Which would not even be an issue, if Lisp, Scheme and Prolog had not lost their aura among AI devs.

Julia and Mojo are attempts at solving the "two language problem", which not every Python user actually has -- they're fine doing work exclusively in Python, not even using any of the libraries you're talking about.

Mojo in particular recognized to compete with Python they'd have to be a superset, then they backed of that goal when they realized it would be too hard.

So at the end of the day, Python has a value proposition and it cannot be entirely subsumed by other languages, because those languages make tradeoffs that move away from Python's value.
Python's value is being a portable scripting language, a better Perl, unfortunately some try to do full blown applications with an interpreted language.

Perhaps it's worse that some even succeed in building very complex systems that can handle a lot of load too (see eg. Instagram)? ;-)

Python has a known set of trade-offs, mostly related to loop performance. But if you understand the trade-offs and available mitigations, it should not stop you from building good software. You know, just like any other ecosystem.

> I like Julia approach, compile everything on first launch, then reuse without speed penality, if you change a function, recompile that.

Python already compiles to bytecode (the .pyc files are a cache thereof). It's just that interpreting even the simple bytecode instructions can take dozens of clock cycles each. I imagine that a lot of this is not in the interpreter loop (which has seen quite a bit of optimization, IIRC up to the level of "predictive" gotos within a big switch statement within a loop) but just unwrapping objects and moving values to and from registers, dealing with the fact that there is basically never any cache coherency for anything etc.

Basically I'm not convinced that writing out the set of machine-code instructions needed to interpret the bytecodes would be a big win, because it takes too many instructions for simple tasks.
Python doesn’t really compile to *.pyc. These are just parsed tokens and AST, really not proper machine code.
The Julia approach is the same as BASIC (as originally designed), Lisp, Prolog, as added info.

If you want to use the same code unmodified *and* your code uses type hints, then you should use mypyc [1].

There are times that it generates faster code than Cython! Of course with Cython you can tweak it and push its limits with various optimizations and other techniques, but for using your existing code as it is and gain massive performance improvements, mypyc it's a must!

Code sample:

    import time

    def fib(n: int) -> int:
        if n <= 1:
            return n
        else:
            return fib(n-2) + fib(n-1)


    startTime = time.time()
    fib(35)
    duration = time.time() - startTime
    msduration = duration * 1000.0
    uduration = msduration * 1000.0
    print(f'{duration:.6f} seconds, {msduration:.2f} ms, {uduration:.2f} μs')


    $ python3 mypyfib.py 
    1.452477 seconds, 1452.48 ms, 1452477.22 μs

    $ # the same code compiled with `mypyc mypyfib.py` produces the following:
    $ python3 -c "import mypyfib"
    0.063701 seconds, 63.70 ms, 63700.91 μs
This is huge, if you think about it!

       95.61% reduction in time
     2180.15% increase in performance
       22.80x faster

This is numba?

Yeah, this is numba. I find it really frustrating the extent to which people don't know about it.

Folks, numba is great. To first approximation: write your python function to "look like C"[1] and work over the numpy arrays you probably already have and understand, put a "@jit" decorator on it, and you're done. It JITs and runs your code natively at native performance.

With some extra effort, there are features for SIMD vectorization and thread parallelism, and even GPU backends (that, full disclosure, I've been pretty frustrated by -- but they do work).

[1] Which is to say, don't touch Python interpreter data structures. No dicts or objects or lists or strings, etc... If you're bound by the interpreter[2] you're bound by the interpreter and nothing is going to help you.

[2] A corrolary here is that the kind of C code numba is NOT good for is "following pointers between structs", which is something that can't be expressed in either python or numpy.

> No dicts or objects or lists or strings, etc.

That's a really intense restriction. Sounds like the name fits; it's not general purpose, it's jit for number crunching and little else.

I'm not sure exactly what you mean by "bound by the interpreter" but there's nothing about touching those data structures that requires the interpreter to be involved in most cases. The problem of slow APIs can be solved by the JIT having intimate knowledge of python's internals, can't it?

> That's a really intense restriction.

Is it? An object field access in python is a dynamic hash lookup followed by a method call as a fallback (itself involving hashed lookups up the class hierarchy). That's not an "interpreter vs. native" kind of thing, that's just the semantics of the language that have to be preserved. And that's just not going to be "fast" in the way that the user of a JIT would want. Code dominated by Python datastructures is going to be "slow" in ways that JITs can't fix, ever.

Which is why Python appears to have given up on the effort in this space. PyPy too[1] really never delivered on the desired performance gains (like 5x or so on typical code) without forcing the user into careful optimization.

Numba, to its credit, doesn't even try. It falls back to python if it must for python stuff, but is quite clear that it's providing no benefit if that's what you're doing. And the stuff it does do is obvious and clean and extremely useful.

[1] PyPy is also looking pretty moribund recently.

A hash lookup can be very fast.  There's no reason for it to be slow when it doesn't need to invoke the fallback.  JITs can't remove the slowest case but they can make the normal case very fast.  Saying it can't be fast ever is a huge cop-out.

Yes, Python's hash lookups are actually pretty good. The comments in the implementation are an interesting read.

But that doesn't help much if/when you're doing two hash lookups per iteration just to find two small integers to add together.

> Saying it can't be fast ever is a huge cop-out.

Maybe, but the world is still waiting for the counterexample. Python is simply not a runtime well-suited to optimization.

In the meantime, those of us who actually enjoy real HPC problems are using numba and rolling our eyes about all the confuffery around JITs. Maybe one will arrive that proves us wrong, but numba is fast today.

LuaJIT has the same dynamism with dictionaries and it's very fast at accessing them in JIT code.

I don't have enough experience with PyPy to say much about it.

I have moved my more complex scripting from Perl/PHP/Python to Lua for a lot of reasons. One being that Lua (even PUC Lua) is a good deal faster than Python (or /bin/sh); another is that, if I want even more speed, I can use LuaJIT (which keeps me stuck at Lua 5.1, but Lua 5.1 is perfect for my needs).

I wish Lua 5.1 could become part of POSIX; there are a lot of implementations of it out there.

Yeah, this is sort of the disconnect. Lua is a fast dynamic interpreter, sitting well above Python but rather below e.g. V8 in its ability to run scalar code over "interpreter types" like doubles and strings and vectors and hash tables.

The upthread comment was about an idea for "inline Cython", which was then hijacked because that's largely what numba is. These are technologies aimed at optimized native code running over native types to do stuff like numerics and ML and other HPC tasks. Lua isn't any more responsive to this domain than Javascript has been, it's not really the subject under discussion.

LuaJIT handles double, strings, and dictionaries at near C level performance. Also, arrays, but Lua’s data model has dictionaries and arrays be the same data structure. Lua 5.1 (i.e. LuaJIT) only supports double numeric types,[1] and its strings are immutable.

Lua 5.1’s edge over Javascript and Python is that it’s a lot smaller and simpler.

[1] It’s possible to recompile Lua 5.1 to have the numeric data type be an int, but the standard compiles of Lua5.1 only have double precision floats for numbers. Bitwise operators are technically not part of Lua 5.1, but a library to add support is easy and is usually done: Most Lua5.1 forks including LuaJIT and MediaWiki’s version of Lua5.1 have such a library available. Later versions of Lua have both int and float support.

> LuaJIT handles double, strings, and dictionaries at near C level performance.

Yeah, but again you don't reach for C when you have a string or hash-based logic problem, which is the reason that other platforms are favored. You reach for Python[1] to solve those problems, and it works fine.

You reach for C when you care about cache footprint or memory layout. You reach for C when you need SIMD parallelism. You reach for C when you care about doing the math in single precision or 32 bit integers and will handle the precision worries yourself.

You emphatically don't reach for python (or Lua) in those situations. But notably you can reach for numba, and implement your small core of performance code in python next to the other logic you already have. And there's value there.

Screaming about using Lua instead is just nonresponsive. Lua is arguably better at performance code than Python. Lua is absolutely not faster than numba, nor will it ever be (absent a numba-like translation layer) and repeatedly trying to argue so is very much missing the point.

[1] Or fine, Lua or JS or whatever. But I'm trying deeply not to let this turn into a frothing language flame, and this is after all a python discussion.

> Screaming about using Lua instead is just nonresponsive.

The point of those comments is not to hype Lua, it's to show what a JIT can do.

The idea is that a python JIT could be just as good as Lua for the parts that aren't suited to numba.

> Lua is absolutely not faster than numba, nor will it ever be (absent a numba-like translation layer) and repeatedly trying to argue so is very much missing the point.

Nobody is arguing that. People are agreeing that numba is fast, but they also want other non-number-crunching things to be fast. It's "yes, and". They're not missing the numba point, they're agreeing and you're missing the additional point they're responding with.

If you're saying V8 is quite fast why did you say the world is "waiting for a counterexample" to JITs on very dynamic objects being slow?

When OP wrote "inline Cython" they didn't seem focused on numerics, they talked about "proper C speed", and they mentioned modifying the language. I don't think it's getting off-topic to suggest a deeper integration that lets the JIT be very intimate with the interpreter and truly inline things in a way that bypasses language-crossing and type-dispatching overhead. As long as you're in the hot path, let it look up object fields in a couple instructions.

> When OP wrote "inline Cython" they didn't seem focused on numerics, they talked about "proper C speed"

Isn't that basically what I said? Lua isn't "proper C speed", nor is PyPy, the cancelled Python JIT in question, nor even V8. That's a different problem area with different technologies. PyPy's problem with slow startup is, in principle, easily fixable.

When it was created, PyPy did not seek to optimise startup performance. Instead, its aim was steady-state performance of JITed code, and it succeeded handsomely. A conceptually simple fix would be to optimise traces in one processor core, while the interpreter runs in another. But PyPy is currently a sequential system and making it parallel, while conceptually easy, is a lot of work and needs a rewrite of the whole system. The other of PyPy's big performance issues (Python code using a lot of FFI calls via a suboptimal FFI) is also, in principle, easily fixable. But this is a social problem: the Python community would have to move towards better FFIs.

While I don't disagree with you in principle, the context for JS JIT vulns and potential Python JIT vulns is pretty different and worth taking into consideration.

For JS, your machine running untrusted JS code is the intended use case. In this scenario the JS is sandboxed in whatever JS engine (V8 etc) and does not have access to "dangerous" methods, and the main use case for a JIT vuln is to escape this sandbox to execute code on the host. This applies to regular internet browsing (and visiting potentially malicious sites) and also, e.g., using the built-in browser in a locked down device (such as game consoles) to gain arbitrary code execution.

For Python, this security boundary doesn't exist. I can't really think of a scenario where you would be running potentially malicious Python code in CPython that would need a JIT vuln to escape whatever sandbox it is in instead of, say, calling the functions in Python directly (or using the C FFI to do whatever). I'm sure that in some niche use cases, this scenario might exist, but to me, it seems like the potential attack surface is fairly minimal.
